pages.lead: Our reverse osmosis (RO) and electrodeionization (EDI) skids make Purified Water (PW) below the USP <645> limit of 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C and the USP <643> limit of 500 ppb total organic carbon (TOC), with no regeneration chemicals. We size each skid at your lowest feed temperature, wet test it at factory acceptance testing (FAT) and ship the installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) protocols with it.

blocks.h: Margin at the generator protects the point of use
body: PW is the bulk water for non-parenteral formulation, the final rinse of most cleaning cycles and the feed to Water for Injection (WFI) stills and Pure Steam generators. USP and Ph. Eur. apply their limits at the point of use, after storage and distribution have had their effect.

So the generator's job is margin. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) taken up through a tank vent raises conductivity. A loop that warms in summer adds microbial risk. We size the skid so its outlet sits well below the limit you release against under the worst feed water of the year, and we show that margin at FAT and again at site acceptance testing (SAT).

The same RO and EDI platform can be built for hospital reprocessing water under CSA Z314, laboratory water under ASTM D1193 and industrial demineralized water. This page describes the pharmaceutical build.

blocks.h: How water moves through the skid
blocks.caption: Pretreated feed arrives softened and free of chlorine and chloramine. A heat exchanger brings winter feed up to membrane design temperature. The first RO pass removes most dissolved ions, organics, particles and bacteria. Carbon dioxide passes RO as a gas, so we convert it with caustic dosing or strip it with a membrane degasser before it loads the EDI. A second RO pass, where your feed needs one, adds margin on conductivity and silica. EDI polishes the permeate in an electric field, with no acid or caustic regeneration. Water below the conductivity setpoint goes to storage; anything above it diverts until it recovers.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: What does FAT prove if the skid runs on your test water, not our feed?
items.a: FAT proves function: every sequence, alarm, interlock and divert, a sanitization cycle reaching temperature at every probe, instrument loop checks and outlet quality on our test water. Performance on your feed water is proven at SAT and OQ. We write the protocols so your quality unit can leverage FAT results in qualification, in line with ASTM E2500 and ISPE commissioning and qualification guidance, where it accepts that approach.

items.q: How do you handle cold feed water in winter?
items.a: RO output falls as water cools. A membrane array rated at 25 °C can lose a third or more of its output at 5 °C, and many Canadian supplies reach that in winter. We size the array at your lowest recorded feed temperature, or add a heat exchanger that holds a design temperature, and we show the capacity at both ends of your range in the mass balance.

items.q: Why EDI instead of mixed-bed ion exchange?
items.a: EDI regenerates continuously in an electric field. There are no acid or caustic deliveries, no regeneration downtime, no resin exhaustion events to investigate and no resin beds for bacteria to colonise between exchanges.

items.q: Single or double pass RO?
items.a: Your feed water decides. High alkalinity, dissolved solids or silica, or a WFI still or Pure Steam generator downstream, point to double pass. Soft, low-alkalinity feed that makes PW only usually suits a single pass ahead of EDI. We show both options against your analysis when the choice is close.

items.q: Our municipal supply is chloraminated. What changes?
items.a: Chloramine must be removed before the RO, because polyamide membranes do not tolerate it. Breaking it releases ammonia. RO rejects ammonium well, but if we raise pH to control carbon dioxide, more of it becomes dissolved ammonia gas, which passes the membrane and reaches the EDI. So we design the chloramine removal and the CO₂ strategy together. Pretreatment covers the removal step.

items.q: Hot water or chemical sanitization?
items.a: Hot water at 80 °C or more leaves no residual to rinse out and test for, and the cycle is proven by temperature at the coldest point. Chemical sanitization suits membranes that are not rated for heat, but adds a residual test to every cycle. Sanitization frequency is set from your trend data during PQ, not fixed at design.

items.q: Can the same skid feed a WFI still or a Pure Steam generator?
items.a: Yes. We size it for your PW draw plus the still or generator feed demand, and design to that equipment's feed limits, typically on conductivity, silica, chloride and total hardness. Those limits go into the functional specification so they are tested at FAT.

items.q: Our feed comes from a private well. Is that a problem?
items.a: Not in itself. USP and Ph. Eur. require PW to be made from water of drinking water quality, so you need to show your well meets it. Iron, manganese, hardness and silica then drive the pretreatment, and we ask for analyses from more than one season because well chemistry moves.

pages.eyebrow: WATER FOR INJECTION · DISTILLATION · USP <85> · PH. EUR. 0169
pages.headline: Water for Injection by distillation, with endotoxin margin you can show an inspector
pages.lead: The multi-effect and vapour compression stills we supply make hot Water for Injection (WFI) below the USP <85> bacterial endotoxin limit of 0.25 EU/mL and the USP <645> conductivity limit of 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C. We set the still's endotoxin reduction against your Purified Water (PW) feed, choose the still type on your steam, power and cooling water costs, and ship the factory acceptance test (FAT) report and installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) protocols with it.

blocks.h: Distillation removes endotoxin by phase change. The margin depends on your feed.
body: WFI is the solvent for parenteral products and the final rinse for product-contact equipment. A still makes it by boiling PW, separating droplets from the vapour and condensing the vapour. Ph. Eur. 0169 asks for exactly that: a still fitted with an effective device to prevent the entrainment of droplets.

A still reduces endotoxin by a fixed factor, not to a fixed level. The FDA Guide to Inspections of High Purity Water Systems notes that many still fabricators guarantee only a 2.5 to 3 log reduction, and describes stills that periodically produced WFI above 0.25 EU/mL because their feed was not treated well enough. So we design the still and the PW system that feeds it as one: the guaranteed reduction factor sets the endotoxin target for your PW, and both go into the functional specification.

Distillation also delivers WFI hot. EU GMP Annex 1 (2022), adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119 and in force since 1 April 2024, gives constant circulation above 70 °C as an example of storage and distribution that minimizes microbial growth. A still fills a hot loop without reheating.

blocks.note: Limits as the pharmacopoeias state them for WFI in bulk, applied at the point of use. Annex 1 paragraph 6.15 expects continuous Total Organic Carbon (TOC) and conductivity monitoring on WFI systems. Your alert levels are set from qualification data and reassessed on trends.

blocks.caption: PW is preheated by the distillate and fed to the first column, where plant steam boils it. The pure vapour from each column, after droplet separation, heats the next column and condenses there as WFI. Vapour from the last column condenses in a cooling-water condenser. Concentrated feed carrying the rejected endotoxin and solids leaves to drain from the last column. Distillate below the conductivity setpoint and above the temperature setpoint goes to storage; anything else diverts to drain.

blocks.h: How a vapour compression still works
blocks.caption: Feed water boils in the evaporator. The vapour passes a droplet separator, then a compressor raises its pressure and temperature so it can condense on the other side of the same heat transfer surface, boiling more feed as it does. The condensed WFI and the blowdown preheat incoming feed. Plant steam or electric heaters bring the still to temperature at start-up; after that the compressor supplies most of the energy, and little or no cooling water is needed.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: Why distil when Ph. Eur. now allows membrane WFI?
items.a: Since April 2017, Ph. Eur. 0169 accepts reverse osmosis coupled with other suitable techniques, and USP has long accepted any process equivalent or superior to distillation. Distillation still makes sense when you want hot WFI for a hot loop, when your contamination control strategy relies on the longest inspection record, or when steam or cheap power is on hand. Membrane WFI saves energy where ambient storage suits your process. We model both on your data when the choice is close.

items.q: How much endotoxin reduction can we count on?
items.a: Only what the still manufacturer guarantees, which FDA's inspection guide puts at 2.5 to 3 log for many stills. A 3 log still fed at 250 EU/mL would deliver WFI at the 0.25 EU/mL limit, with no margin. So we set an endotoxin target for the PW feed well below that, and design the PW system and its sanitization to hold it.

items.q: What feed water does the still need?
items.a: PW for a multi-effect still, plus the manufacturer's limits on silica and hardness, which scale hot surfaces, and on chloride, which attacks stainless steel at still temperatures. Vapour compression stills often accept softened or RO feed. We write the feed limits into the functional specification and size the PW skid to meet them.

items.q: Does an imported still need a Canadian registration number?
items.a: Yes. Pressure vessels and fittings installed in Canada need a CRN under CSA B51 from the province of installation, and a still designed for another market may need design changes before it is accepted. We include registration in the project schedule from the start. [Confirm Aquemi's CRN process and the provinces covered.]

items.q: What happens at start-up and shutdown?
items.a: Every start-up diverts distillate to drain until conductivity and temperature reach setpoint. The condenser and distillate line drain on shutdown. FDA's inspection guide describes a still whose condenser held about 50 litres of WFI for up to several days between runs, a source of endotoxin; we design so that cannot happen.

items.q: Can the still feed a hot loop directly?

pages.headline: Water for Injection by membrane, with the control strategy your inspector will ask for
pages.lead: Our double-pass reverse osmosis (RO), electrodeionization (EDI) and ultrafiltration (UF) skids make Water for Injection (WFI) at ambient temperature, below the USP <85> bacterial endotoxin limit of 0.25 EU/mL and the USP <645> conductivity limit of 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C, with no plant steam for generation. We design the biofilm and endotoxin controls the EMA expects from a non-distillation system into the skid, and tell you plainly when distillation is the better route.

blocks.h: The limits are the same as distilled WFI. The evidence you owe is not.
body: USP defines WFI as water purified by distillation or by a process equivalent or superior to distillation in removing chemicals and microorganisms. Since 1 April 2017, Ph. Eur. 0169 also accepts a purification process equivalent to distillation: reverse osmosis, single-pass or double-pass, coupled with other appropriate techniques such as EDI, ultrafiltration or nanofiltration. EU GMP Annex 1 (2022), adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119, repeats that wording in paragraph 6.10.

Conductivity, Total Organic Carbon (TOC), endotoxin and microbial limits do not change with the route. What changes is the burden of proof. A still removes endotoxin by phase change at high temperature. A membrane system runs at ambient temperature, which the EMA's 2017 questions and answers on non-distillation WFI (EMA/INS/GMP/443117/2017) call an ideal environment for biofilm. So the EMA expects a documented control strategy, developed alongside the design, that shows how the system prevents, detects and removes microbial growth and endotoxin.

Ph. Eur. 0169 also asks that notice is given to the manufacturer's GMP supervisory authority before a membrane WFI system is implemented. USP has no such step. We build the system and the evidence together, so the control strategy, the qualification plan and the notice your regulatory team files draw on the same documents.

blocks.h: How water moves through the skid
blocks.caption: Pretreatment delivers feed that is softened and free of chlorine and chloramine, checked by an oxidant sensor before the first RO pass. Two RO passes in series remove dissolved ions, organics, bacteria and endotoxin. Carbon dioxide passes RO as a gas, so we convert or strip it between the passes before it loads the EDI. EDI polishes conductivity with no regeneration chemicals. The final UF membrane is the last barrier to endotoxin and bacteria. Water below the conductivity and TOC setpoints goes to storage; anything else recirculates or diverts until it recovers. The whole train is hot water sanitized on a schedule set from your data.

blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Will Health Canada and the FDA accept membrane WFI?
items.a: Both inspect against the pharmacopoeia you release to, and USP has allowed WFI by any process equivalent or superior to distillation for many years. Health Canada recognizes USP and Ph. Eur. as Schedule B publications, and its GUI-0119 adopts Annex 1, which names RO coupled with EDI, UF or nanofiltration. Acceptance rests on your data: a sound design, a documented control strategy and a PQ that covers seasonal feed changes.

items.q: Who do we notify, and when?
items.a: Ph. Eur. 0169 asks that notice is given to the manufacturer's GMP supervisory authority before implementation. The EMA questions and answers say that for a site outside the EU it is the authority of the EU importer's Member State, or, where a mutual recognition agreement covers the product, the site's own authority. Your regulatory team confirms which applies to your products and files the notice; we supply the design and control strategy documents behind it.

items.q: Is membrane WFI as safe on endotoxin as a still?
items.a: It can meet the same limit, by a different mechanism. A still relies on one phase change; a membrane system relies on several barriers in series and on keeping them intact and clean. That is why we trend rejection and differential pressure, integrity test the UF, and sample endotoxin after the UF throughout PQ. If your feed carries a high or variable endotoxin load, we say so and model distillation too.

items.q: How long does qualification take?
items.a: Longer than many teams plan for. The EMA questions and answers describe daily sampling at all points in the initial phase, then performance shown over an extended period, typically a year. Most plants start using the water once the initial phase is complete, on a decision their quality unit documents. Build that year into the project schedule from the start.

items.q: Can we store membrane WFI hot?
items.a: Yes. Annex 1 gives circulation above 70 °C as an example of storage that minimizes microbial growth, not a requirement. Heating ambient WFI to fill a hot loop gives back much of the energy saving, so most membrane WFI plants use an ozonated or regularly sanitized ambient loop instead. Storage and distribution covers both.

blocks.h: Pure steam is qualified on two sets of tests, and only one is about the generator
body: Pure steam sterilizes product-contact surfaces directly: porous and hard-goods loads in autoclaves, vessels and transfer lines by SIP, and stoppers in processors. EU GMP Annex 1 (2022), adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119 and in force since 1 April 2024, sets two requirements for it in paragraph 6.17. The condensate must meet the current WFI monograph of the relevant pharmacopoeia, with microbial testing not mandatory. And the steam must be assessed periodically for non-condensable gases, dryness value and superheat against validated parameters.

The first set is chemistry. USP Pure Steam tests the condensate for total organic carbon (TOC), conductivity and, where the steam is used to make parenterals, bacterial endotoxin below 0.25 EU/mL. The generator controls these: droplet separation keeps feed water and its endotoxin out of the steam, and feed degassing keeps dissolved carbon dioxide (CO₂) from raising conductivity.

The second set is physics, and EN 285 gives the acceptance criteria most sterilizer manufacturers and inspectors use. These tests are made at the sterilizer. A generator that delivers dry, gas-free steam at its outlet can still fail them at the point of use if the header collects condensate, leaks air in during shutdown, or reduces pressure in one large step. So we design, test and document the generator and its distribution together.

blocks.h: How a pure steam generator works
blocks.caption: PW is preheated and vented, so dissolved air and CO₂ leave before evaporation. Plant steam or electric heaters boil it in the evaporator, on the far side of a double tube sheet. Pure steam leaves at a controlled pressure, through a sample cooler, to a drained and insulated header. Blowdown removes the concentrated feed.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: Our sterilizer fails the dryness test. Is it the generator?
items.a: Usually it is the header. Condensate that collects in flat or sagging runs, missing or failed traps, damaged insulation and dead legs all produce wet steam at the sterilizer from a generator that tests dry at its outlet. We survey the header and the generator together, test at the generator and at the sterilizer, and the difference tells you where the water comes from.

items.q: Does the condensate really have to meet WFI?
items.a: For steam that sterilizes materials or product-contact surfaces directly, yes: Annex 1 paragraph 6.17 asks for condensate that meets the current WFI monograph, without microbial testing. USP Pure Steam applies its 0.25 EU/mL endotoxin limit when the steam is used to make parenterals. Steam that only heats jackets or coils, without product contact, can be plant steam; your contamination control strategy should say which users are which.

items.q: EN 285 is a European sterilizer standard. Does it apply to us?
items.a: EN 285 is written for large steam sterilizers, and its steam quality clause gives the acceptance criteria for gases, dryness and superheat. Annex 1, which Health Canada applies as GUI-0119, names the same three parameters but sets no numbers, so most sites and sterilizer manufacturers use the EN 285 values. If your sterilizer manufacturer specifies different limits, we design to the stricter of the two.

items.q: How often do we have to test?
items.a: Annex 1 asks for a sampling schedule that obtains representative steam regularly and for periodic assessment of the physical parameters. It sets no interval. A common approach is condensate chemistry and endotoxin quarterly, non-condensable gases quarterly until the data support a longer interval, dryness annually, and superheat watched continuously from pressure and temperature. Your validation plan sets the actual frequency.

items.q: What feed water does the generator need?
items.a: USP allows pure steam to be made from drinking water, but feed impurities concentrate in the evaporator. Silica and hardness scale the heat transfer surface, chloride attacks stainless steel at these temperatures, and CO₂ and ammonia raise condensate conductivity. We feed from PW or RO permeate and write the feed limits into the functional specification, so blowdown and cleaning intervals are predictable.

items.q: Where does superheat come from?
items.a: Mostly from reducing the pressure of dry saturated steam in one large step, or through a small orifice close to the sterilizer. Superheated steam behaves like hot air until it cools to saturation, so sterilization is less effective. We stage pressure reduction and place it far enough upstream for the steam to return to saturation before the sterilizer.

items.q: Can we use our WFI still instead of a separate generator?
items.a: Often, yes. The first column of a multi-effect still can deliver pure steam, with WFI output reduced while it does. It suits small or intermittent steam demand. A separate generator is the better choice when sterilizers and SIP run while WFI demand is high, or when you want to maintain one without stopping the other.

pages.headline: Storage and distribution loops that deliver generator quality at the furthest point of use
pages.lead: We design and build tanks and loops for Purified Water (PW) and Water for Injection (WFI) that keep flow turbulent at peak draw, as EU GMP Annex 1 paragraph 6.9 requires, hold every branch to the ASME BPE dead leg target of a length-to-diameter ratio (L/D) of 2 or less and drain completely. Hot WFI loops circulate above 70 °C (Annex 1, 6.10); ambient loops are sanitized by heat or ozone on a schedule you can defend. Every slope, weld and branch is recorded on the as-built isometrics your validation team qualifies against.

blocks.h: Water is released at the point of use. That is where the loop is judged.
body: USP and Ph. Eur. apply their PW and WFI limits to water as it is used, after it has sat in a tank and travelled through tens or hundreds of metres of pipe. A generator that makes water well below the limit gives you margin. The storage and distribution system decides how much of that margin reaches the furthest valve.

Most microbial excursions that trace back to the loop have the same short list of causes: a branch that holds still water, a run that does not drain, flow that drops to laminar when several valves open at once, a wet vent filter, or a sanitization cycle that never reaches the coldest point. EU GMP Annex 1, which Health Canada applies as GUI-0119, names most of them directly: drainable slopes and no dead legs (6.7), turbulent flow that is monitored (6.9), heated and integrity-tested vent filters (6.11) and sanitization on a predetermined schedule (6.12).
We design against each of those causes, then record the evidence on drawings and test reports, so the question an inspector asks about any branch has an answer on paper.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: Does a WFI loop have to be hot?
items.a: Not by rule. Annex 1 paragraph 6.10 gives constant circulation above 70 °C as an example of storage that minimizes microbial growth, not the only acceptable method. Ambient WFI loops with ozone or periodic heat sanitization are in use, but your contamination control strategy has to justify the choice and your monitoring data has to support it. Where a still delivers hot WFI, a hot loop is usually the simplest to defend; with membrane WFI, the energy case often favours ambient storage. We set out both for your demand.

items.q: Which L/D do you design to, and how do you measure it?
items.a: L/D ≤ 2, the ASME BPE target: L from the inside wall of the main pipe to the valve seal point, D the inside diameter of the branch. It applies to instrument tees and sample valves as well as points of use. The older six-diameter rule comes from the FDA's 1993 inspection guide, which notes it was developed for hot 75–80 °C systems; we do not design to it. Every branch is listed with its L/D in the dead leg register.

items.q: How do you keep flow turbulent when several points of use open at once?
items.a: We take the worst-case combination of outlets from your survey, not the average, and size the pipe and pump so the return stays turbulent with all of them open. A variable speed pump holds return flow or pressure as demand changes, and a low-return-flow alarm tells you when it cannot. At SAT we open the worst-case outlets together and record the return flow, which gives you the qualified flow rate Annex 1, 6.9 asks you to monitor.

items.q: Ozone or periodic heat for an ambient PW loop?
items.a: Ozone keeps the tank under continuous control and sanitizes the loop without heat cycles or insulated piping, at the cost of ozone and UV monitoring, ozone-compatible seals and an extra test after each sanitization. Periodic heat needs no residual test but takes the loop out of use for each cycle and needs heating capacity. Your utilities, your tolerance for downtime and any existing equipment usually decide it; we show both against your schedule.

items.q: How do you prove there is no ozone at the point of use?
items.a: An ozone sensor after the UV destruct unit is interlocked to stop supply if ozone breaks through, and the UV intensity is monitored. After each loop sanitization the water is tested for residual ozone before the loop returns to use, in line with Annex 1, 6.12, which asks for water to be tested after disinfection. The interlock is tested at FAT and OQ.

items.q: How should points of use be sampled?
items.a: The way the water is used. The FDA inspection guide says that if a hose is usually attached, the sample should be taken at the end of the hose, and flush times should match production practice. Annex 1, 6.13 asks for a sampling programme that covers all outlets and points of use at a specified interval, with at least one representative sample every day of water used in manufacturing. We place sample valves for the return and the tank, and write point-of-use sampling into the PQ protocol.

items.q: What about rouge?
items.a: Rouge, the iron oxide film that forms on stainless steel, is found mainly in hot WFI and pure steam systems and in systems with frequent heat cycles. On its own it does not usually move conductivity or TOC, but loose rouge that migrates is a particle risk, and your quality unit will expect it to be inspected and trended. We limit the causes at design (finish, passivation, chloride control during construction, pump selection), give you inspection points at the tank and pump, and plan derouging and repassivation as maintenance rather than an emergency.

items.q: Can you add points of use to an existing loop?
items.a: Yes, after a hydraulic check of the whole loop at the new peak draw. Each new branch is cut in with a zero-static valve, orbitally welded, passivated and added to the isometrics and dead leg register, under your change control, with a requalification scope agreed before work starts. Shutdown length depends on the tie-ins: [typical shutdown for a point-of-use addition, days]. See upgrades and requalification.

items.q: Can the loop connect to a generator from another supplier?
items.a: Yes. We define the interface in the functional specification: water quality and flow at the tank inlet, the signals exchanged, and how a generator divert or a low tank level is handled, so the loop and the generator are qualified as one system.

pages.eyebrow: PRETREATMENT · USP <1231> · HEALTH CANADA · US EPA NPDWR
pages.headline: Pretreatment that keeps chlorine, chloramine and scale off your RO membranes in every season
pages.lead: USP <1231> requires the feed to a Purified Water (PW) system to meet drinking water standards, such as the US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (NPDWR) or, for most Canadian sites, the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality. Drinking water is not reverse osmosis (RO) feed. We design the pretreatment train from your water data across the seasons, so the RO inlet sees no detectable chlorine or chloramine, a silt density index (SDI) of 3 or less and hardness the membranes can live with, and the carbon bed is sanitized so it does not become the source of your bioburden.

secondary_cta.label: RO fouling or chlorine breakthrough now? Request service

blocks.h: Drinking water standards protect people, not membranes
body: Every pharmacopoeial water starts as drinking water. USP <1231> sets the NPDWR, or equivalent EU, Japanese or WHO drinking water rules, as the minimum quality of the source. Ph. Eur. asks for water intended for human consumption. In Canada your municipality treats to the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality and its provincial regulation. Meeting that standard is your starting point and, for a private well, something you have to show.

Those standards are set for health and taste, and they allow water that damages RO membranes. The NPDWR allows a chloramine residual up to 4 mg/L as Cl₂. Health Canada sets no limit for chloramine at all, because at drinking water levels it is not a health concern. Polyamide RO membranes are typically rated for less than 0.1 mg/L free chlorine. Hardness has no health limit; a few milligrams per litre of calcium in the RO concentrate is enough to scale it.

Pretreatment closes that gap. It also creates a risk of its own: once the carbon removes the disinfectant residual, nothing in the water holds bacteria back. So we design removal and microbial control together, and we monitor the outlet that your validated system depends on.

blocks.h: Canadian feed water: what changes, and what it does to your RO
rows: Many large municipal utilities use chloramine as the residual disinfectant in the distribution system. Some switch temporarily to free chlorine for system maintenance.
Oxidizes polyamide RO membranes. Reacts slowly on standard carbon. Breaking it releases ammonia, which can reach the EDI.
Carbon contact time sized for chloramine, catalytic carbon or bisulfite, total chlorine measured at the RO inlet, and an ammonia and CO₂ strategy agreed with the PW skid design.
Surface water intakes can fall to near 2 °C in winter and pass 20 °C in late summer.
Cold water cuts RO output and lowers silica and calcium solubility. Warm water speeds bacterial growth in carbon beds and softeners.
Membranes sized at your coldest month or a feed heat exchanger, scaling checked at both ends of the range, sanitization frequency set for summer.
Rivers and lakes carry more turbidity, colour and natural organic matter in the freshet and when lakes turn over.
Higher SDI and total organic carbon (TOC) foul membranes and load the carbon. TOC at the RO inlet moves TOC at the PW outlet.
Media filter sized for the worst month, SDI tested on site, ultrafiltration where SDI cannot be held by media alone.
Great Lakes water is moderately hard. Many groundwaters in Ontario, the Prairies and Quebec are much harder.
Calcium carbonate scales the last RO elements. Alkalinity becomes carbon dioxide that loads the EDI.
Duplex softeners regenerated on measured hardness, concentrate Langelier saturation index (LSI) checked, alkalinity handed to the PW skid's CO₂ removal.
Higher in groundwater and some prairie and Shield-region surface water.
Silica passes softeners. It scales RO concentrate, limits recovery and loads the EDI and any still downstream.
Recovery limited by silica at your coldest feed, antiscalant where projections need it, and silica in the feed limits of the WFI still or Pure Steam generator.
Mostly well water, sometimes in older municipal mains. Health Canada sets an aesthetic objective of 0.1 mg/L for iron and a maximum acceptable concentration of 0.12 mg/L for manganese.
Oxidized iron and manganese foul membranes and coat softener resin, often at levels drinking water allows.
Oxidation and catalytic media filtration ahead of the softener, sized on analyses from more than one season.
Every dechlorinated train, worst in summer and after low-flow weekends.
Carbon beds and softeners grow biofilm that sheds into the RO and raises bioburden in PW.
Hot water sanitizable carbon, sampling before and after each bed, and continuous flow or recirculation at no demand.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: Is pretreatment part of the validated system?
items.a: It depends on where your risk assessment draws the boundary. Many sites qualify from the RO inlet onward and treat pretreatment as supporting equipment under good engineering practice. Its performance still decides whether the RO meets its limits, so we document it to the same standard, test it at FAT and SAT, and supply installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) protocols where you bring it into scope.

items.q: Do we have to prove our feed water meets drinking water standards?
items.a: USP <1231> expects you to know that it does. For municipal supply, the utility's reports plus your own periodic testing at the plant inlet are the usual evidence. For a private well you are the utility, so you need a sampling programme against the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality or the NPDWR, including microbiological tests. We can propose the parameters and frequency.

items.q: Our municipality uses chloramine. Is standard carbon enough?
items.a: Usually not at a reasonable bed size. Chloramine reacts on carbon far more slowly than free chlorine, and slower still in cold water. We size catalytic carbon or two beds in series on contact time at peak flow and winter temperature, or dose bisulfite, and measure total chlorine at the RO inlet, because a free chlorine analyser does not see chloramine.

items.q: What happens to the ammonia from chloramine?
items.a: Removing chloramine releases ammonia. RO rejects it well as ammonium, but at the higher pH used to control carbon dioxide more of it is dissolved ammonia gas, which passes the membrane and loads the EDI. So the chloramine removal here and the CO₂ strategy on the PW skid are designed together. See Purified Water generation.

items.q: Why do our carbon bed counts spike?
items.a: Carbon removes the disinfectant and adsorbs organics, so it grows biofilm, faster in summer and when flow stops. Counts after the bed that rise between sanitizations usually mean the interval is too long, the bed stagnates at no demand or the media is exhausted. We trend counts before and after the bed and set sanitization from that data.

items.q: Why measure SDI on site rather than from the utility report?
items.a: Utilities report turbidity, not SDI, and SDI depends on what the water picks up between the treatment plant and your tap. ASTM D4189 measures it in 15 minutes at your cartridge filter outlet. We test during the feedwater review where we can, and again at SAT.

items.q: Can we keep our existing pretreatment when we replace the RO?
items.a: Often, if it meets the new RO inlet targets. We review its sizing, media age, sanitization capability and monitoring against your feed data, and tell you what to keep, upgrade or replace. See upgrades and retrofits.

items.q: Our utility switches to free chlorine for a few weeks each year. Does that matter?
items.a: Yes, in both directions. Free chlorine reaches the carbon at a higher oxidant level, and the switch back changes what the bed must remove. Ask your utility for its schedule; we design for both disinfectants and alarm on total chlorine at the RO inlet.
